Eco-Friendly Retail Design — Final Diploma Project 2023 — Eco-Friendly Retail Design — Final Diploma Project 2023 — Eco-Friendly Retail Design — Final Diploma Project 2023 — Eco-Friendly Retail Design — Final Diploma Project 2023 —

This project is centered around the intersection of eco-friendly retail design and the challenges faced by small brands looking to create sustainable spaces. Throughout my research and development, I explored innovative approaches to creating modular, reusable materials that could not only enhance the aesthetic appeal of retail environments but also significantly reduce environmental impact.

This focus on sustainability allowed me to integrate ecological principles into every aspect of the design process, from material selection to functionality. By drawing inspiration from nature and considering the limitations of smaller budgets, I aimed to create retail spaces that are both cost-effective and environmentally conscious.

Who is —

Sasha
Bouquin
Sagot

Sasha Bouquin Sagot is a visionary fashion designer whose work emphasizes the fusion of practicality and aesthetic in modern clothing. His approach to fashion design is rooted in functionality, prioritizing the needs of travelers, explorers, and workers who seek durable, versatile, and stylish garments.

Drawing inspiration from a multicultural environment, Sasha's designs embody the balance between the urban and the natural world. From Marseille's bustling cityscape to the serenity of natural landscapes, his collections reflect a deep connection to the environment and a focus on creating clothing that serves real-life purposes.

His work is currently showcased at FRAP STORE, a collaborative space in Marseille where local creators can display their collections, making Sasha a key figure in this vibrant urban fashion hub.

Context —

The FRAP
Store

Sasha Bouquin Sagot's latest retail project is set within the vibrant and culturally rich FRAP STORE in the heart of Marseille, near the Vieux Port and La Canebière. This space serves as a collaborative platform for local creators, blending urban influences with the independent spirit of the designers it hosts.

The FRAP STORE, known for showcasing unique pieces that reflect the creative pulse of Marseille, has become a fitting venue for Sasha's innovative approach to functional, urban-inspired fashion.

05
Three pillars —

Design
Axes

DURABLE
Sustainable retail design plays a crucial role in promoting environmental responsibility, reducing the carbon footprint of stores through the use of recycled materials, energy-efficient technology, and eco-friendly construction methods. Brands like Patagonia and The Body Shop serve as examples of how embracing sustainability can enhance brand reputation while also benefiting the planet.
RE-USABLE
Retail spaces are designed with the circular economy in mind, focusing on reusing materials and reducing waste. This strategy not only cuts down on environmental impact but also provides financial benefits for brands by lowering the need for new resources. Examples such as Allbirds and Reformation showcase how reusing materials can lead to creative and unique design solutions.
MODULAR
The modular design approach prioritizes flexibility and adaptability, allowing spaces to be easily rearranged and adjusted according to the needs of the brand or retailer. With references from notable brands such as Nike and Muji, this axis emphasizes efficiency, sustainability, and an engaging customer experience.

1. Experimentations —

Nature
& Flowers

This research aims to create a series of artistic 3D renderings that bring nature back into the center of the retail space, presenting it as a work of art to capture every detail and draw full attention to it.

Building on the concept of nature-inspired creations, I explored ways to highlight the intricate details of plants that we may have seen before but never truly observed. I collected samples of plants and flowers, scanned them, and used them as the basis for graphic designs.

08
2. Modular Design —

Thinking
& Making

In my exploration of innovative ways to create a sustainable retail space, I focused on modular elements, their patterns, and the potential design applications. The repetition of a pattern to make surfaces adaptable led me to question the aesthetic and functional possibilities of modular designs.

The challenge I faced was to create modular components that could be assembled into different types of furniture, adaptable to the needs of various stores or retail spaces. I worked with simple patterns, utilizing materials I had available, such as architectural model wood.

While conducting this experimentation, I questioned the accessibility of wooden slats and developed an alternative using a more readily available material: pallet wood.

1/1 Size Adaptation

The furniture's design is now adaptable to the size of the pallet wood planks, further contributing to its versatility and sustainability. The purpose of this furniture is to create an interactive installation where customers can engage with and test the materials used in SBS's creations. The furniture includes a space for a basin or container filled with water, soil, or sand, and pieces of fabric will be available for customers to immerse, soil, and test for durability. This installation fosters a connection between the creator and visitors, enhancing customer interest by allowing them to actively participate in the project.

09
3. Re-use Waste —

Green
Wall

The idea of a green wall made from recycled plastic bottles offers another fascinating exploration of material reuse. By stacking plastic bottles, perforating them to allow for plant growth, and supporting them with a wooden or metal frame, a sustainable, eco-friendly wall can be created.

This concept involves selecting suitable plants, implementing an efficient irrigation system, and enhancing the aesthetic with natural materials like moss or cork. This project merges innovation with sustainability, demonstrating how waste materials can be transformed into functional design elements that support ecological principles.

01
Proposition —

MODULAR
RETAIL SPACE

In this design proposition, I applied a modular system within the retail space, incorporating wall-mounted panels, modular furniture, and movable shelves that can be adjusted according to the store's needs.

On certain walls, photos from the collection's photoshoot are projected, eliminating the need for prints, reducing costs, and minimizing environmental impact. The use of projectors also allows for greater flexibility, as the images can be changed or animated to adapt to the space.

The modular furniture placed in the center of the room invites customers to test the durability of the clothing by submerging textiles in water or subjecting them to wear and tear. This interactive element fosters a sense of connection and involvement with the brand.

1. Sustainable Material —

Material
Research

In today's ecological context, I found it necessary to question how materials in retail design can contribute to the environmental crisis. This led me to experiment with the creation of my own material, made from recycled waste.

The objective was to create a strong material from waste or recyclable elements — specifically paper, cardboard, flour, clay, and plant matter — to form durable volumes suitable for displaying items.

Thermoformed plastic molds were used to test how the material would set and if it could take on the desired shape. The molds were made using plants and vegetation, placed under heated plastic to capture their form and replicate it. The results showed that the material on its own is sturdy enough to maintain its shape without the need for cardboard reinforcement.

Through incorporating natural elements, I wondered if entire plants could be adhered to the creations. The mixture worked well as an adhesive, allowing for playful experimentation with colors and the potential to create patterns on walls or objects.

I also considered whether moss could be attached to this mixture — to create a green wall or add moss to a display resembling a rock. The objective was to test if the material, once dried, could support the moss and withstand misting without decomposing.

02
Proposition —

NATURE
AS RETAIL

This design proposition is centered around placing the clothing in its intended environment: nature. The goal was to bring nature into the retail space, utilizing the techniques developed during my experiments. I focused on creating mini biomes, small areas with different environments, to contextualize the clothing designs and highlight their functionality.

These biomes can be constructed using the materials developed, combined with cardboard, onto which plants like moss can be adhered, and dead tree trunks or other plant matter can be added to replicate a natural setting.

Additionally, a faux stone wall can be installed, featuring a mannequin to display the collection. Given that the collection is also inspired by rock climbing, S. Bouquin-Sagot suggested incorporating climbing ropes into the space.

14

This project successfully merges nature and retail design, creating an immersive, eco-friendly experience that showcases both sustainability and functionality. Placing the clothing in its true environment while encouraging customer interaction and providing valuable insights into how sustainable practices can enhance both aesthetics and practicality. Ultimately, the project demonstrates a nature-inspired approach to retail design.
